8d166c32ef:
How to turn a prompt into a decision boundary you can state, measure and tune.

Part one covers explicit criteria for precision:

  • why “be conservative” and “only high-confidence findings” don’t work;
  • what a false positive costs in developer trust;
  • how to write report-if rules, skip rules and severity anchors with code;
  • how to measure precision per category;
  • how to switch noisy categories off while you fix them.

Part two covers few-shot prompting:

  • how to pick two to four examples at the ambiguous edge of the rules;
  • how to show the reasoning;
  • how to test that the examples teach the rule and not the surface;
  • how the same technique stops an extractor from inventing values for fields that are absent.
516b1256a3:
Everything else in this chapter follows from that.

  • “Be conservative” fails because it names a direction without a dimension. So the model supplies its own prior, which is the thing that produced the noise in the first place.
  • A confidence cutoff fails because confidence isn’t the variable that separates your noise from your defects.
  • False positives matter more than their count suggests, because developers respond to the noise rate. Once they stop reading, even the correct findings are lost.
  • Severity needs code, because otherwise “high” is a mood.
  • Disabling a noisy category works because precision is a property of a category, not of the whole bot.
  • Few-shot works because a demonstration fixes concrete points on both sides of a boundary that a sentence can only gesture at. It reduces fabrication in extraction because it shows that “null” is a legal answer for this kind of document.
2bfccba1f8:
For task statement 4.1, the exam guide lists the importance of explicit criteria over vague instructions, and the effect of false positives on developer trust. The skills are:

  • writing specific review criteria that say which issues to report (bugs, security) and which to skip (minor style, local patterns);
  • temporarily disabling high false-positive categories while the prompts are improved;
  • defining explicit severity levels with concrete code examples.

For 4.2, the guide says few-shot examples are the most effective technique for consistent output when detailed instructions alone are inconsistent. The skills are writing:

  • two to four targeted examples for ambiguous scenarios, showing why one action was chosen over the alternatives;
  • examples that show the exact output format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix);
  • examples that separate acceptable patterns from genuine issues, so false positives fall while the model still generalises to similar patterns;
  • examples for extraction that cover varied document structures and the correct handling of missing or informal values.

I’ve paraphrased the wording. The bullets below are the checklist this chapter teaches, with the section where each one is taught.
d964aab1d9:
Two other chapters pick up where this one stops. Chapter 12 is how you make the output valid: tool use with a JSON schema, optional fields, validation and retry. This chapter is how you make it right once the shape is already valid. Chapter 13 is how you run the reviewer at scale and in more than one pass: the Message Batches API, independent reviewer instances, per-file and cross-file passes.

Where a section depends on one of them, I say so, and section 18 collects the cross-references. Chapter 3 matters too, for the opposite reason. A prompt is a probabilistic control, and anything that must hold every time belongs in a hook.
5087c22d5b: Both halves of this chapter are old ideas in new clothes, and the history explains the exam’s emphasis. The first half is a problem every automated reviewer in software engineering has met: static analysis tools that people stop trusting. The second half is the discovery, around 2020, that you can teach a language model a task by showing it a handful of examples in its input.
097d72f155:
Stephen Johnson’s lint (Bell Labs, 1978) was one of the first tools to read C source and warn about code that compiled but looked wrong. The warnings were heuristics: patterns that are often bugs and sometimes not.

Programmers quickly found out what happens to a tool that cries wolf. It gets turned off, or filtered through a shell pipeline that removes most of its output, or run once and forgotten. Every static analyser since has been built with that lesson in mind. In a mature analyser, most of the engineering effort goes into suppressing warnings, not into finding more of them.
4bdfd78994:
When analysers moved from research prototypes to products run on millions of lines, the companies that built them wrote down what they’d learned.

The Coverity team’s 2010 article in Communications of the ACM, “A few billion lines of code later”, describes their experience selling a static analyser. They report that a false-positive rate much above 20 to 30 per cent makes users stop believing the results. They’d rather miss real bugs than flood users with doubtful ones.

Google’s Tricorder (published in 2015) built the same trade into its design. An analyser is allowed into the code review pipeline only if its “effective false positive” rate is low; the paper sets a target of 10 per cent. “Effective” means reviewers didn’t find the result useful, not that the analysis was technically wrong.

That definition matters here. For a PR bot, a comment is a false positive if the developer wouldn’t act on it, whatever its technical truth.
cb39a78ec3:
Two practices from that era carry straight over to LLM reviewers.

First, categories are first-class. Each check has an owner, a measured precision, and a switch. A check with poor precision is turned off for everyone until it’s fixed.

Second, feedback is part of the product. Reviewers can mark a result “not useful” with one click, and that signal is the measurement.

The “temporarily disable high false-positive categories” in task statement 4.1 is this practice, applied to prompts. (I’m citing both papers from memory of their main claims. If you want the exact figures, read the originals.)
54147350c4:
GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020, “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners”) reported something that surprised the field. A large enough model could perform a new task if the prompt contained a task description and a few demonstrations, with no change to its weights. The paper separated zero-shot (description only), one-shot and few-shot (typically ten to a hundred examples in a short context). That’s the origin of the term the exam uses.

Later work showed that the model takes partly the format and the label space from the demonstrations, and partly the mapping itself. Results can also swing with the choice and order of examples.

The practical consequence is the one this chapter keeps returning to. Examples are an input to a classifier, so you choose, test and version them like any other input.
f0cd8f8652:
Instruction-tuned models (InstructGPT, 2022, and the assistants that followed) made zero-shot prompting usable. You can describe the task and get a reasonable answer. That shifted the role of examples. They stopped being the only way to explain the task, and became the way to settle what the description leaves open.

Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) added a second use. An example that contains the intermediate reasoning, not just the answer, improves the model’s handling of cases that need a step.

Current Anthropic guidance describes examples as one of the main ways to steer format and tone. It recommends wrapping them in tags, so the model can tell them from instructions. And it says relevant, diverse, clearly delimited examples work best. The number it suggests is three to five, against the exam guide’s two to four. Check the docs for the current wording, because this guidance is revised with each model generation.
f7015bb59e:
Before any technique, fix the vocabulary. The exam’s distractors are mostly confusions between these terms.

A reviewer reads a change and, for each possible issue, makes a yes-or-no decision: report or stay silent. Compare those decisions to what a careful human would conclude, and you get four counts:

  • A true positive is a real defect that the bot reported.
  • A false positive is a report about something that isn’t a defect (or isn’t worth the developer’s time).
  • A false negative is a real defect the bot missed.
  • A true negative is correct silence.

True negatives are by far the largest cell in a real PR stream. That’s why accuracy (correct decisions over all decisions) is a useless metric here. A bot that says nothing is 98 per cent accurate on a stream where 2 per cent of changes contain a defect.
bbbb378be4:
Precision is TP / (TP + FP): of the comments the bot posted, the share that were right. Recall is TP / (TP + FN): of the real problems, the share the bot found. F1 is their harmonic mean, 2PR / (P + R), which punishes a lopsided pair.

You’ll rarely optimise F1 directly, because the two errors have different costs. In a PR reviewer, a false positive costs developer attention and credibility on every PR. A false negative costs one defect, and a human reviewer, tests, or a second pass might still catch it.

That asymmetry is why task statement 4.1 is written about precision. The first thing you do to a noisy reviewer is raise precision, while holding recall as close to constant as you can.
6249ddea40:
Take the scenario this chapter uses throughout. A Spring Boot monorepo for a telecom order-management platform has a CI job that posts Claude’s comments on every PR. After four weeks, you sample 200 comments and mark each as fixed (the developer changed code because of it) or not.

Fifty were fixed. Precision, defined the way Google’s “effective false positive” defines it, is 50 / 200 = 0.25. Of the 150 non-fixed comments, say 120 were style or “consider” suggestions. The other 30 were attempts at real rules that didn’t apply. Across the same PRs there were 60 genuine defects, and the bot commented on 50 of them. So recall is 50 / 60 = 0.83.

The tempting move is to ask the model to be more selective overall. What does that do? If selectivity trims findings in proportion, keeping 60 per cent of everything leaves 30 true and 90 false comments. Precision is still 0.25, and recall has fallen to 0.50.

Now compare that to removing one category. Remove the style category outright, and you drop 120 false positives and no true positives. That leaves 50 true and 30 false: precision 0.62, recall unchanged. Same model, same code. The lever that works is the one that acts on the category boundary.
cd072c3672:
Run the numbers once with your own counts before you believe any advice about prompts. Companion example 02 prints exactly this table.

It also prints the base-rate effect, which is worth knowing for the interview as well as the exam. Take a rule with 90 per cent sensitivity and a 10 per cent false-alarm rate on clean changes. Its precision is 0.90 when half of all changes are defective, 0.50 when one in ten is, and 0.16 when one in fifty is. Real PR streams are in the last regime.

So a reviewer that “looks accurate” in a demo built from defective snippets will be mostly noise in production. That’s another reason to evaluate on a labelled set that includes the clean and near-miss changes your repository actually produces (section 09).
de8a714041:
Every review prompt asks for many small decisions. Is this line a defect? Is this number the total or a subtotal? Is this customer message an escalation? Each decision has a threshold, and a threshold has two properties: where it sits, and along which dimension it’s measured.

“Be conservative” says you want the threshold higher. It doesn’t say which dimension: severity? likelihood? exploitability? how confident the model is that the pattern exists? And it doesn’t say how much higher.

The model has no access to your 200-comment sample, your team’s idea of a serious defect, or the lint rules that already run in CI. It fills the gap with its prior, which is the average of the code-review text it was trained on. That average is full of the kind of comments that annoyed your developers: naming, missing Javadoc, “consider adding a test”. The instruction added no information. So it can’t have moved the boundary to where you wanted it.
03d422b030:
Notice also what “conservative” does when it does have an effect. The model reads it as a general disposition toward saying less. A disposition applies across the board, to correct findings and noisy ones alike, because nothing in the sentence tells them apart. The measured effect is a drop in recall, with precision roughly where it was. That’s the worst of both outcomes.

Companion example 01 shows the pattern on a labelled set of 19 diffs. Precision is 0.45 with a generic prompt and 0.43 with “be conservative”, while recall falls from 1.00 to 0.67. The explicit-criteria prompt reaches precision 0.60 at recall 1.00, before any examples are added.

As the companion README says, that’s a simulation of the mechanism. Take the direction and the reasoning from it. Your own labelled set will give you the real magnitudes.
0c692f35d2:
An explicit criterion replaces an adjective with a test: “report SQL built by concatenating any value that originates from the HTTP request”. That one sentence names the construct (string concatenation into SQL) and the condition (request-derived input). By omission, it also rules everything else out of scope.

You’ve written this kind of thing for years. A Predicate<Finding> in a Drools rule or a Spring Security expression is testable. A comment that says “be careful with user data” is not. The principle is identical. If you can’t write down what makes a change report-worthy, you can’t test whether the system applies it. And you can’t tune it when it’s wrong.
a2c2232902:
The exam doesn’t only apply this to code review. The official sample question about a support agent that escalates inconsistently has the same structure. The instruction “escalate when appropriate” leaves the threshold to the model. The right fix is explicit escalation criteria (customer asks for a human, policy gap, no progress) plus a few examples. Not sentiment analysis, and not a confidence score.

For extraction, the equivalent vague instruction is “be accurate” or “extract the total”. Neither says which of three numbers on the page is the total.

Whenever a stem describes inconsistent judgement calls and one option replaces an adjective with a stated test, that option is almost always the intended answer.
aece7a6b29:
“Only report findings you are highly confident about” sounds more technical than “be conservative”, because it names a quantity. It’s just not the quantity you need.

A model can be very confident that a missing final modifier or an absent Javadoc comment is worth mentioning. It has seen thousands of reviews that said so. The noise you want to remove is a category of comment, and confidence is a property of an individual statement. The two don’t line up. The model’s confidence about a stylistic remark is as high as its confidence about a SQL injection, so a cutoff removes both kinds in the same proportion.
bcb5f22d7e:
Using self-reported confidence as a control has three further problems.

It is uncalibrated. A model saying “0.9” doesn’t imply that 90 per cent of such statements are right. The relationship differs by category and by model, so you’d need a calibration set per category to use it.

It is unstable. The number depends on phrasing and on the surrounding text, and it moves between runs.

And it is not an input to anything you control. If you ask for it and filter on it, you’ve built a second, hidden decision boundary that nobody wrote down. That’s exactly the situation explicit criteria are meant to remove.

The exam guide makes the same point twice in its reliability domain. Self-reported confidence is an unreliable trigger for escalation (task 5.2). Field-level confidence is useful for routing extractions only after it has been calibrated on a validation set (task 5.5). Here it’s the same finding from another angle.
a09b36ba71:
So the exam treats two options as traps in this family: “instruct the model to only report high-confidence findings” and “add a confidence threshold and suppress findings below 0.8”. Both appear in the guide’s own statement of what does not improve precision.

A third, quieter trap is “ask the model to rate each finding’s importance from 1 to 10 and drop anything under 7”. It’s the same idea with a different scale.

If an option relies on a number the model emits about its own output to separate good from bad, be suspicious. The reliable separation comes from a category you defined, a rule id the model must cite, and a measurement you took from outside the model.
fe52ab9f04:
Why does the guide say false positives “erode trust in the whole tool” rather than “waste time”? Because a PR reviewer isn’t read once. The same people read it on every PR, and each reader updates a belief about whether the next comment is worth their attention. That belief is the tool’s real resource.

Picture a developer who opens a comment and spends two minutes finding it doesn’t apply. Then they see the same kind of comment on the next PR. They become less likely to open the one after. After enough rounds, the probability is low enough that they resolve comments in bulk.

The bot is still running, and its raw recall is unchanged. But its effective recall, the share of real defects that lead to a fix, has gone to nearly zero.
23f332b9aa:
You’ve seen this mechanism in operations. A pager that fires on every CPU spike teaches the on-call engineer to acknowledge without reading, and the one real page in the pile is missed. In clinical settings it’s called alert fatigue. Published studies of hospital alarm systems report that clinicians override a large majority of drug-interaction alerts.

The mechanism doesn’t depend on the technology. It depends on the ratio of useful to useless interruptions a person experiences, and on how slowly that person’s trust returns when the ratio improves.
229d40edee:
Two details of the model matter, even though its numbers are invented.

First, the noise rate drives the decay, not the noise count. A bot that posts twelve comments with precision 0.8 loses almost no trust. One with precision 0.25 loses most of it within ten PRs.

Second, recovery is slower than decay. In the simulation, read-probability falls from 0.70 to 0.14 over twenty noisy PRs, and climbs back only to 0.30 over twenty clean ones.

That asymmetry is why the guide recommends acting early and visibly. Disable the noisy categories now, keep the precise ones running, and tell developers what changed. Don’t wait for a perfect prompt.
e2fd7f95f8:
None of this says recall doesn’t matter. A reviewer that never reports anything has perfect precision (vacuously), and it’s useless. The point is the exchange rate.

A missed defect is one defect, in a pipeline that has other defences: human review, tests, a second pass (Chapter 13). A noisy bot degrades the one defence that depends on people reading it.

So in a first fix, you accept a small recall loss to buy a large precision gain. Then you plan to win the recall back with better criteria and examples, not with volume. The exam asks you to recognise this order of operations: stop the bleeding by category, then improve.
2901f5f605:
Explicit criteria have three parts, and the exam rewards answers that contain all three:

  • a report-if list of concrete constructs and conditions;
  • a do-not-report list of the categories that generate noise;
  • severity anchors written as code.

A fourth element is structural, not semantic. The model must tie every finding to a rule id. Then code can drop anything outside the criteria, instead of trusting the model to obey. Here is the scenario prompt first as it’s usually written, then as it should be.
e8c9b5d6ac:
Each rule in the prompt answers four questions:

  • Construct: what shape of code are we talking about (string-built SQL, a catch block, a transactional method)?
  • Condition: under what circumstance does that construct become a defect (the concatenated value is request-derived; nothing logs, rethrows or converts the exception)?
  • Exemption: what looks similar but is fine (a constant in the SQL, a re-interrupt, a call after commit)?
  • Evidence: what must the finding quote so a reviewer can verify it (the offending line, and a one-sentence reason tied to the rule)?

Draft rules usually give the first question and half of the second. The exemption is where most false positives come from. It’s best written as an example, which is why the anchors carry a non-example next to each example.
949789503a:
Two points about the skip list.

First, it names categories with a reason (“Spotless and Checkstyle enforce these”). A reason lets the model extend the exclusion to near neighbours you didn’t list, such as import grouping or brace style, because it understands why the category is excluded.

Second, the exam guide’s phrase is “minor style and local patterns”. A local pattern is a convention this codebase chose deliberately, and that a generic reviewer would flag. For example, the order platform might return Optional.empty() for “not found” after logging, by design. Or it might use a project-wide Result<T> wrapper instead of exceptions. Without a way to say so, the bot will suggest “idiomatic” alternatives on every PR.

Put local patterns in a short, versioned document that the prompt references or includes. In Claude Code in CI, the natural home is the project’s CLAUDE.md, or a review-conventions file it imports. (The CI chapter and task 3.6 cover how CI gets its context. Check the docs for the exact mechanism in your version.)
b93eee4a0e:
The sentence “an empty list is a good result” isn’t decoration. A model asked to review a diff has a mild pull toward producing at least one finding, because a review with no findings feels like failing the task. Say that an empty result is correct, then demonstrate it with an example (section 12), and the pull goes away.

The rule-id requirement has a second purpose: it makes the output auditable. You can check a finding that cites R3 against R3’s text. A finding with no id is outside the criteria, and post-processing can discard it. That’s a deterministic guarantee no prompt wording gives you.

Chapter 12 shows how to make the id a required field in a tool schema, so the shape can’t drift. Companion example 05 shows the semantic half: it rejects ids that aren’t enabled, and replaces the model’s severity with the rule’s.
f85b2a1050: The explicit prompt is a Spring Security expression, not a log line. @PreAuthorize("hasRole('AGENT')") states a test over named inputs, and you can unit-test it. “Only let appropriate people in” you can’t. Wherever you’d have written a rule in Drools or a Specification<T>, write a rule in the prompt. Give it an id, and test it against labelled cases.
d2c0add49a:
A severity label is a promise about what happens next. Say “HIGH” blocks the merge and “LOW” is a note. Then a model that labels by feel will block merges for style and wave through an injection.

The exam guide’s remedy is to define each level with concrete code examples. The reasoning is the same as before. A word like “critical” is an adjective, and the model interprets an adjective through its prior. A level defined as “the reviewer can cite a call path from an external input to the sink” is a test.
40ad8df571:
Two questions generate a usable ladder:

  • What is the worst realistic consequence if this is a true finding: data exposure, data corruption, lost failure signal, maintainability cost?
  • How directly is it reachable: from an external request, from an internal job, only under a rare configuration?

A high-consequence, directly reachable defect is HIGH. A real defect with a recoverable consequence is MEDIUM. An actionable deviation with no operational consequence is LOW.

For each level, and for each rule where it matters, write one short code example that’s clearly at that level, and one look-alike that isn’t.
4f6917e026: Notice that every non-example is something a reasonable reviewer might flag. Two of the four (the enum constant in R1, the re-interrupt in R3) came from false positives in the sample, not from imagination. That’s the right source: write anchors and exemptions from the failure log. A severity ladder invented at a whiteboard tends to describe the cases you already handle.
72b681b5c2:
Left to itself, a model drifts upward on severity, for the same reason a junior reviewer does: calling something HIGH feels safer than calling it LOW. In a long diff you’ll see six HIGHs and nothing that actually blocks.

Three controls stop this:

  • The ladder is written as consequences with anchors, so “HIGH” has a specific meaning.
  • Severity is looked up from the rule (the guard above overwrites the model’s value). For the cases the rules cover, that removes the degree of freedom entirely.
  • The harness maps severity to action. So the worst a mislabelled finding can do is trigger the action for its rule, not an arbitrary one.

Some rules really do need case-by-case severity, say a data-exposure rule where severity depends on the field. For those, put the decision procedure in the rule: “HIGH if the field is in the PII list in section X, else MEDIUM”.
06832b3f23: A decision to disable a category, add an example, or ship a prompt change needs numbers. And the numbers need to be per category, because an aggregate hides everything that matters. The four-week sample had overall precision 0.25. Broken out by rule, it looked like this. The aggregate is the weighted mean of very different things.
fd7cd560f1:
Use two sources together.

Production feedback is the cheap one. Each bot comment gets a developer outcome: fixed in a follow-up commit, resolved without change, dismissed, thumbs-down. It measures effective precision, the quantity that drives trust. But it’s slow, and biased toward comments people read. It says nothing about recall, because you only see the findings that were posted.

A labelled set is the controlled one: a few dozen to a few hundred diffs, each with the set of rule ids a careful human says should be reported. Build it from three kinds of case, in this order of importance:

  • near misses: code that looks like a rule but is fine. This is where false positives live.
  • genuine defects: one or two per rule, plus mutated variants.
  • style-only changes, where the correct output is empty.

Add every production false positive to the set as it appears. This is the stratified sampling the exam guide describes in its reliability domain. Sample by category, because the aggregate masks per-type failure.
d2ae964d81:
Recall needs a different trick, because you can’t count the defects nobody noticed. Seed them. Take clean commits, inject known defects (a mutation of the R1 pattern, an empty catch), and measure the share the bot finds.

Seeded recall is optimistic, since seeded bugs are easier than real ones. But its direction is reliable. For a prompt change, the question is usually “did recall drop”, not “what is the absolute recall”.
a8382d3e4d:
The arithmetic has two traps. A rule that hasn’t fired has no precision, only an undefined ratio. Don’t report it as 1.0. And the unit of analysis is a comment, not a PR. One PR with ten bad comments from one rule counts ten times against that rule, because it cost the developer ten interruptions.

The interval matters, because decisions get made on small counts. Seven fixes out of twelve is a precision somewhere between 0.32 and 0.81. Set a minimum sample before you switch a rule off or on; 30 is a reasonable floor for a first decision.
0bbaa7eff5: Per-rule outcomes make a natural Micrometer counter: reviewer.comments{rule="R3",outcome="fixed"}, incremented from the PR webhook handler. A Grafana panel then shows precision per rule over time. An alert on “precision below floor with n at least 30” triggers the disablement process in the next section. The same counters give you the before/after comparison when a prompt change ships.
98242bba61:
The guide’s most operational sentence for 4.1 is that you can temporarily disable high false-positive categories to restore developer trust while you improve the prompts for those categories. Read each clause.

  • “Temporarily” means there’s an owner and an exit criterion. It’s not a quiet deletion.
  • “High false-positive categories” means the unit is a category with a measured precision. That’s why section 09 comes first.
  • “To restore trust” names the reason. What you’re protecting is the reader’s willingness to keep reading.
  • “While you improve the prompts” says the work continues offline.
64ca43872e:
The alternatives to category-level disablement are all worse, and the exam offers each one as a distractor.

Turning the whole reviewer off removes the R1 and R2 findings that developers do act on. You lose recall to fix a precision problem in one category, and you also lose the habit of reading the bot’s output.

Capping comments per PR (“at most three”) drops comments by an arbitrary rule. Ranked by the model’s confidence, it keeps nits and cuts defects. Companion example 17 shows one real defect in the top three of nine.

Raising a global threshold trims every category together, as section 03 showed.

Disabling the one category that fails is the only option that acts at the grain where the problem exists. Example 17 measures the kill switch against the single-rule disable: recall 0.00 for the first, and 0.67 at precision 1.00 for the second.
3db2f54f79:
Implement disablement as configuration. The prompt is rendered from a rule table in which each rule has a status. Disabling R3 is a one-line change. It removes the rule text from the live prompt and records why. The rule’s text and anchors stay in the repository for the offline work.

Don’t comment the rule out of a prompt file. Comments rot. And a disabled rule that’s still half-present in an example will keep influencing the model: a few-shot example that shows an R3 finding teaches R3, whatever the rules list says. So remove the examples that belong to a disabled rule, too.
6b5b6f6767:
Shadow mode is the step that makes re-enabling safe. The rule runs on real PRs, and nothing is posted. Its findings are stored with the outcome a human would have chosen. You can collect that by sampling, or by checking whether the code at that line changed. When shadow precision clears the floor on enough samples, the rule goes live.

Skip that step, and the first evidence about the repaired rule is another round of noise. It lands on the developers who just got relief from the first.
0ab06d97cf:
Two housekeeping points.

Tell the developers. A one-line note on the bot’s summary comment (“Exception-handling checks are paused while we improve them”) turns an unexplained change into evidence that someone is listening. That’s half of the trust recovery.

And time-box the pause, with a named owner. A category that stays disabled for six months is a deletion nobody approved.
47fd51ff51: Treat review rules like feature flags in Spring Cloud Config or a flag service. The rule text is versioned code. The enabled flag is runtime configuration with a recorded reason. Shadow mode is a dark launch. Re-enabling is a progressive rollout gated on a metric, not a quiet edit. The instincts you apply to a risky new endpoint apply to a risky new rule.
b9dab31975:
A few-shot prompt contains worked input and output pairs before the real input. The model conditions on them the way it conditions on everything else in its context. From the pairs, it infers what the task is, what the output should look like, how much detail is wanted, and what rule maps those inputs to those outputs.

Instructions describe the rule in words. Examples demonstrate it. When the rule is crisp (“return JSON with these four keys”), a description is enough, and examples just add cost.

When the rule is fuzzy, it’s different. Think of what counts as actionable, whether this sentence is an escalation request, or which of three amounts is the total. There a demonstration transfers more information than a paragraph. It fixes concrete points on both sides of the boundary, and a boundary is exactly what a description can’t pin down.
f3ee4d48f7:
That’s why the guide calls few-shot the most effective technique for consistent, formatted output when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results. Read the condition. The guide doesn’t say to reach for examples first. It says that once you’ve written the detailed instructions and the results still vary, examples are the lever that works. “Still vary” means the format drifts, borderline cases flip between runs, or the same document is read two ways.

The exam’s wrong answers for such stems are “write longer instructions”, “add more rules”, “lower the temperature”, and “run it three times and take the majority”. The first two add description to a problem that description hasn’t solved. The third and fourth reduce variance around a boundary that’s in the wrong place, or missing.
91a003621f:
Put them where they’re stable and unmistakable. For a reviewer or extractor with many calls, the examples belong in the system prompt, next to the criteria they illustrate. Wrap them in <examples> and <example> tags, and keep them visibly separate from the live input. The live input goes in the user turn, in its own tag (<diff> or <document>). The Anthropic prompting guidance recommends this separation, so the model can tell examples from instructions and from the task.

The alternative is to supply them as earlier user and assistant turns, so the conversation itself demonstrates the behaviour. That works. But the examples then sit in the message history, where they’re easier to trim by accident and harder to version with the rules.

For a per-request tool, the system-prompt form is easier to reason about. It has a second advantage too. A long, stable prefix is exactly what prompt caching is for, so the cost of carrying a few kilobytes of examples falls sharply once the prefix is cached. (Minimum cacheable length and prices change; check the docs.)
21d001bbf4: The guide’s wording is specific: two to four targeted examples, for ambiguous scenarios, that show why one action was chosen over the alternatives, and that separate acceptable patterns from genuine issues. Each qualifier rules out a common mistake.
d9258678ab: Few, not many. You pay for every example on every call. Every example also pulls the output toward its own surface features: its length, its number of findings, its wording. Two to four well-chosen examples define the format and the boundary. The tenth example of the same kind adds cost and drift. The general Anthropic guidance suggests three to five; the exam guide says two to four. Treat both as a range for a first draft, and let a labelled set decide your number. Add examples until held-out results stop improving.
bace7ad785: Ambiguous, not obvious. The model already handles the clear cases. An example of "... where id=" + req.getParameter("id") teaches it nothing it didn’t know. An example where the concatenated value is a compile-time constant teaches exactly where R1 stops. Pick from the failure log: the cases the prompt gets wrong today.
f78951ecaf: Contrast pairs. Put an acceptable case beside a similar-looking genuine issue. The difference between the two is the lesson. The pair also prevents the opposite failure, an exemption that grows too wide. The ORDER BY example below is the genuine twin of the enum-constant example.
6ab1decd67: Varied. Use different rules, different lengths, different surface forms. Examples that all look alike teach the surface (“the total is always the last number”, “there are always two findings”).
e0c6a830d3: Synthetic or anonymised. An example containing a real customer’s MSISDN will sooner or later be echoed into another customer’s output. Use made-up data in prompts.
82b05e2282:
The practical procedure is mechanical:

  1. Run the current prompt on the labelled set (and on production false positives as you collect them).
  2. Group the false positives by rule and by cause: why the rule fired when it shouldn’t have.
  3. Take one case from each group. If there are more than four groups, fix the most frequent four first. More than four examples costs tokens and rarely helps.
  4. Add a genuine finding as the contrast for the most subtle exemption.

Companion example 10 does the grouping, and finds four causes in the sample: a constant in SQL (three cases), a re-interrupt, a class-level authorization check, and a call placed after commit.
7b5bad8d13:
For the order-management reviewer, this procedure produced an example block with four examples:

  • the enum constant (empty);
  • the ORDER BY (finding, as its contrast);
  • the re-interrupt (empty);
  • the access-failure-to-empty conversion (finding, as the contrast for R3).

Two empty and two non-empty. Here it is as it appears in the prompt.
19d62602ac:
Measured on the labelled set in the simulation, the criteria-only prompt gives precision 0.60 at recall 1.00.

Adding these four examples gives 0.82. They fix the enum, ORDER BY and re-interrupt cases, and the held-out constants. But two near misses (the class-level authorization and the after-commit call) are still reported, since no example covers them.

Replacing the set with one mined from all the near misses in the failure log reaches 1.00 on this set. Read that last number as a warning, not a result. It’s measured on the same cases the examples came from. Section 14 is about not fooling yourself with it.
a8cebb649c:
The guide asks for examples that show why one action was chosen over the alternatives. An example with only an input and an output tells the model what to do for that input. An example that also contains the reason tells it what to do for inputs that share the reason, including ones you didn’t show.

In the reviewer set above, the enum example’s reason is “the concatenated value is a compile-time constant, so R1, which needs request input, does not apply”. A model that learns that sentence can handle Constants.DEFAULT_REGION or a private static final String TABLE without ever seeing them. A model that learns only “empty findings for PlanStatus.ACTIVE.name()” has learned a string.
b208bca7c8: A reason field in the output contract. The model emits <why> or a reason per finding, as in the examples above. The harness reads it, uses it to build the PR comment, and logs it for audit. It’s a deliverable, not a scratchpad. So keep it short and about the rule, not a narrative.
11cce68d28: Reasoning before the verdict. In free-text outputs, put the reasoning ahead of the conclusion in the example. A model that writes its verdict first commits to it, and then rationalises. When you need only the verdict, put the reasoning inside a tag you strip (and see the next point).
7969c7e466: Examples that shape the model’s own thinking. With extended or adaptive thinking enabled, worked examples in the prompt shape how the model reasons in its thinking blocks. The Anthropic guidance says each example works best presented as a problem, the method to apply, and the expected answer. It prefers general instructions (“think thoroughly”) over hand-written step lists. The same guidance warns that some current models may decline a prompt asking them to write their reasoning out in a tag, and tells you to rely on thinking instead. Behaviour differs by model generation here. Check the docs for the model you’re using before you design the output contract around visible reasoning.
7d7fded3c2:
Reasoning in examples has costs and risks.

  • It adds tokens to each example (cacheable, as discussed).
  • It gets imitated. If your reasons are always one sentence, the model’s will be too. If they’re sloppy, the model’s will be sloppy.
  • A reason that cites the wrong cause is worse than none. An example whose says “because it is in a test file” teaches the model to skip test files.

Review the reasons the way you review the rules. And test what an example actually teaches by perturbing the input (section 14).
1e45551a0e: The exam’s own sample question about inconsistent escalation has the same structure, and it’s a good place to see reasoning pay off. The agent escalates some customers who didn’t ask for a human. And it fails to escalate one who asked twice. The fix is explicit escalation criteria, plus a few examples whose reasons name the criterion that decided the case.
886ebf97be:
Notice that the second example is the important one for the failure described. It’s the “angry but resolvable” case, and its reason states the principle that sentiment isn’t a trigger.

This is also why the exam rejects “add sentiment analysis to decide escalation”. Sentiment correlates with the right answer, but it isn’t the criterion. The examples show the criterion.
eaac00d0e3:
The guide says examples that distinguish acceptable patterns from genuine issues should reduce false positives while enabling generalisation to similar patterns. Both halves are testable, and both can fail.

An example set can fix the cases it contains, and only those. That’s memorisation. Or it can teach the rule, so unseen look-alikes are handled correctly. There’s also a failure in the other direction: an exemption learned too broadly turns into false negatives.
387dddc0b3:
Three habits make this concrete.

Hold out cases. Never evaluate on the examples. Reserve a set of near misses and defects that appear nowhere in the prompt. The companion keeps five: two constants that should be skipped, and three defects that should be reported.

Perturb the examples. Take an example input and change an identifier, a literal, or the order of two lines. If the prompt’s answer flips, the model learned the surface.

Include held-out positives next to held-out negatives. A prompt that skips constants may also skip String.valueOf(request.getParameter(...)), because it contains a method call that looks like a constant accessor. The held-out defect with a header-derived value (row three in the figure) is there to catch that.
5170f49989: Generalisation also limits how far you should trust an example. A reasoned example transfers to cases that match the reason. It doesn’t transfer to cases that match only its vocabulary. Vague reasons (“this is fine”) transfer unpredictably. Write them as the rule applied: the cause, the rule id, and why the rule doesn’t fire.
6139fe6dec:
Not every few-shot problem is about a boundary. A common complaint is that the findings are correct but unusable. Some have line numbers and some don’t. Some propose a fix and some only complain. Severities come back as “High”, “high” and “P1”.

The guide’s fourth skill is examples that show the exact output format, such as location, issue, severity and suggested fix. It works for the same reason as before. A schema described in words is read loosely, while an example is copied.
b9d8e399e6:
Companion example 11 measures this with a simple proxy: the share of findings that carry exactly the five agreed keys. With a generic prompt it’s 0.00. With a prompt that describes the keys in words, it’s 0.67. With the examples, it’s 1.00. The numbers come from the simulation’s drift model, so take the ordering, not the values.

In real use you see the same three-level pattern. The middle level is the dangerous one. The prompt looks specified and mostly works, and the failures are the rare keys that go missing in the long tail.
cf50e50ac4:
Actionable is part of the format. A comment that says “this is vulnerable” makes the developer do the diagnosis. A comment that names the construct, the input that reaches it, and a concrete change doesn’t.

Put a suggested_fix in every non-empty example, and show a fix that’s a small, specific edit, not a rewrite. If your examples contain fixes of different sizes, the model’s fixes will vary the same way.
442257eb24:
Chapter 12 covers using a tool with a JSON schema (and tool_choice forcing it) to make the output syntactically valid. There, the model can’t return a missing bracket or an unknown key. That removes shape errors that examples only reduce.

What the schema can’t do is make the content correct. A schema allows "severity": "HIGH" on a style nit. A required total_due field forces a number even where the document has none.

The two techniques complement each other, and the exam likes stems that combine them. Use the schema for shape, and criteria and examples for semantics. If the choice is “examples or schema” for a formatting problem, the schema is the stronger tool for syntax, and examples are the stronger tool for what goes in the fields. For the field-level design that makes null expressible (optional fields, an "unclear" enum value), read chapter 12 next.
ce5a243132:
In extraction, the dominant failure isn’t inconsistency. It’s invention.

Ask a model for the invoice date from a page with no invoice date, and it will often return a date anyway. There’s a date on the page (the due date, the statement timestamp, the billing period). The task said “date”. And returning a value feels like doing the job. The same happens with totals (the previous balance is the largest number), with invoice numbers (a circuit id looks like an identifier), and with measurements (“about two weeks” becomes 14).

The model isn’t lying. It’s producing the most helpful-looking completion. The fix has to make “not present” an equally natural completion.
0de5eb4653:
Both are about what the examples must show.

An extractor whose examples are all one-page invoices, with the total at the bottom, learns “the total is the last number”. The first summary-first statement breaks it: the page begins with Previous balance 14,330.00.

The guide’s phrase “examples for varied document structures” means choosing examples that differ in the structural cues that matter. Where does the field sit, and how is it labelled? Is it in prose or a table, in a header or a footer? Does it span pages? The same document family will contain narrative text, tables, and cross-references (“see page 3”). Each is a different way for a value to be present or absent.

And “correct handling of missing information” means at least one example whose correct output is null, with a note explaining why. That gives the model a demonstrated way to say “not here”.
1e6a9bc5d0:
Companion example 14 runs seven document layouts (21 fields) through three prompts in the simulation:

  • The bare prompt gets 15 of 21 right, and hallucinates 6 values.
  • Adding the instruction “use null if not present” gets 17, and hallucinates 4. The instruction removed the obvious inventions (a fabricated invoice number) but not the plausible ones (a due date taken as the invoice date, the largest number taken as the total).
  • Adding the three examples gets 21 of 21, with no hallucinations.

The pattern is that the instruction helps and the examples finish the job. That’s what the guide’s sentence “few-shot examples reduce hallucination in extraction” describes. The simulation encodes this; the real numbers are for you to measure on your documents. Why does it hold? An instruction states the rule, while an example shows it applied to the specific look-alike that tempts the model.
98063fa941:
Real documents say “net 30”, “approx. $4k”, “two weeks”, “Q3”, “ASAP”. Decide what the field wants, and demonstrate it.

If the field is a number of days, show “two weeks” becoming 14 and “soon” becoming null. If the field is a canonical amount, show “approx. $4k” becoming 4000 with a precision: "approximate" flag. Or keep the original text in a second field.

The rule of thumb: an informal value is either convertible by a stated rule, or it isn’t. If it is, show the rule applied once. If it isn’t, show null with the original string preserved. Both are examples, not instructions, because the boundary between the two is a judgement call.
03f38481e7:
Examples reduce invention. They don’t eliminate it. Two cheap guards belong in the harness.

First, ask for an evidence quote beside every non-null value. Check that the quote occurs in the source text and contains the value. Reject a value without a quote, or one whose quote isn’t in the document.

Second, validate semantically what you can. The total equals the sum of the line items, within rounding. The date of an invoice isn’t in the future.

Companion example 15 separates what grounding catches from what it misses. It catches a fabricated invoice number, because the string doesn’t occur in the text. It misses a due date used as the invoice date, because that string does occur. That second class is the one the examples are for.
1f33ff27dc:
Chapter 12 builds the other half: a schema in which the absent value is expressible (optional or nullable fields, an “unclear” enum member), semantic validation, and retry with error feedback. A retry fixes a format or arithmetic error. It can’t fix a value the document doesn’t contain, because the information isn’t there to be found. A retry loop that keeps asking will eventually receive a confident invention.

Chapter 13 adds the production pattern for extraction at volume. Refine the prompt on a small sample before submitting a batch. A batch run at half price on a prompt that invents values is a half-price pile of wrong data.

And the exam guide’s reliability domain adds the measurement rule. Validate accuracy by document type before automating, because an aggregate 97 per cent can hide a 70 per cent on one layout.
a922d187e0: Criteria and examples solve different problems, and a production reviewer or extractor uses both. Criteria set scope and precision: what’s in, what’s out, what each severity means. Examples set consistency and edge placement: where the boundary actually falls on messy inputs, what the output looks like, and that empty is allowed. When a prompt misbehaves, the symptom tells you which one to reach for.
0fe0e02ae1:
Order the system prompt so stable, high-value material comes first and per-request material comes last, in separate tags: role and scope, criteria, severity anchors, examples, output contract. Then, in the user turn, the diff.

Stable material first matters for prompt caching, which can only reuse an unchanged prefix. It also keeps the examples near the output contract they illustrate. Per-file calls repeat the prefix for every file, and that’s where caching earns its keep. The 14-file PR in example 18 carries the same roughly 800-token prefix on 14 requests. Exact minimum cacheable lengths, time-to-live and price multipliers change with the model and the plan, so check the docs rather than hard-coding assumptions.
6579ee94c7:
Two sizing notes.

Criteria and examples together often run to a few thousand tokens, so keep them tight. You pay for every added example on each call. And in long, repetitive prompts, the model weighs the instructions at the start less than you’d expect.

Also, don’t put the live diff inside the example block. The examples and the input are different kinds of text. Putting the live input inside the same tag as the examples is one of the commonest ways to get a review of the example instead of the diff.
8a6e4ef758:
The model’s output is an input to code. The harness parses it (a tool schema in Chapter 12 makes this reliable). It applies the guard: rule id enabled, severity from the table, evidence present. It applies policy (severity to action), posts the comments, and records outcomes.

Each step that turns a probabilistic output into a deterministic decision is a place where the system is stronger than the prompt. For example, a review event of REQUEST_CHANGES should depend on whether a guarded HIGH finding exists, not on the model’s overall verdict. The model can be wrong about whether a diff is mergeable, and right about a SQL injection. Code can act on the second without trusting the first.
3e7bdea9dd:
Model the pipeline as a Spring Batch job or a plain @Service pipeline:

  • DiffSplitter;
  • PromptRenderer, which reads the @ConfigurationProperties rule table;
  • ReviewClient, the Anthropic Java SDK or a WebClient call;
  • FindingGuard;
  • SeverityPolicy;
  • PrCommenter.

Each is a plain class with a unit test. Only ReviewClient touches the network, so you test everything else without a model. The companion code uses the same separation.
2e9e66ad23:
A prompt is code that runs on a model, so it needs tests. Those tests split along a line that’s easy to forget.

Some behaviour belongs to your harness, and it’s deterministic. The prompt is rendered from the right rules. A disabled rule is absent. The guard drops an unknown rule id. The severity policy maps HIGH to a blocking review. The grounding check rejects a value that isn’t in the text. These tests run offline against a fake client, in milliseconds, on every commit.

Other behaviour belongs to the model, and you can only observe it by calling the model. Does the explicit prompt really lift precision on your labelled set? Do the examples generalise? Those tests run live and less often. They report numbers with intervals, instead of passing or failing on single cases.
bef778e562:
The companion code is explicit about this line. sim_model.py is a deterministic simulation of the behaviours the chapter describes. The exact numbers it prints (0.45, 0.60, 0.82, 1.00) belong to the simulation.

What those runs verify is that the harness is wired correctly. The rule table renders, the guard drops what it should, the per-rule scoring is right, and the gate fails when a rule is removed.

Run the same scripts with --live and an API key, and they send the same prompts to the real model. Assertions on exact outcomes then turn into reports. That’s how you’d produce the real before-and-after numbers for your own labelled set.
ecd2ecbcf7: Treat the prompt file like source: a change goes through a gate. The gate runs the labelled set and checks per-rule thresholds, because an aggregate lets one rule collapse behind the others. It also counts out-of-criteria comments on the style-only diffs. That count should be zero.
97548f53e5:
Three cautions.

  • A threshold of 1.0 on a small labelled set will flake when you add a hard case. Use the interval from section 09, and move to a percentage as the set grows.
  • A gate on a set that includes the prompt’s own examples overstates quality. Keep the held-out cases from section 14 in it.
  • Pin the model version in the gate run. A prompt tuned against one model generation can behave differently on the next, and the gate is how you find out. (The exam’s configuration domain covers version pinning.)
ab94940818:
Explicit criteria and examples are tools for judgement calls: places where some error is acceptable and precision is a metric. They aren’t tools for guarantees. A prompt has a non-zero failure rate, however explicit it is.

The exam makes this point in the agentic domain with the refund example. If a refund must never happen before identity verification, enforce it in a hook or a prerequisite gate, not in a longer instruction. A reviewer rule like “never approve a change that touches the payments module” is the same. It’s a policy check in CI, not a sentence in a prompt.

Use the stem to decide. Words like “must always”, “never”, “compliance”, “financial” and “regulated” point to code. Words like “inconsistent”, “borderline”, “too many comments” and “judgement” point to criteria and examples.
e62d5d8b7b:
Two links deserve a sentence each.

The detected_pattern field in Chapter 12 lets you do this chapter’s per-category measurement at scale. When each finding names the code pattern that triggered it, you can group the dismissed comments by pattern. Then you find the next example to write without reading each one.

And Chapter 13’s independent-reviewer finding explains why the session that wrote the code shouldn’t apply this chapter’s criteria. A model reviewing its own output in the same context keeps the reasoning that produced it, and is less likely to question it. The reviewer you tune here runs as a separate instance, with its own prompt, on the diff.
08a136dbf1: The questions below follow the exam’s shape: a scenario, four plausible options, one best answer. Decide before reading the reasoning. In this domain, the wrong answers are mostly reasonable engineering ideas that go wrong in one of two ways. Either they replace a stated test with an adjective or a number the model emits. Or they pull a global lever where the problem is local.
c261645f1c:
This is task 4.1 almost word for word. The cause is an undefined boundary. So the fix defines it (explicit criteria, severity anchors), and acts where the measured noise is (the two bad categories) while the precise ones keep running.

A is the instruction the guide says doesn’t improve precision. C answers a specification problem with capacity; a larger model fed the same vague criteria has the same prior. D hides noise by dropping comments arbitrarily. Going by the model’s own ranking, it can drop the security finding and keep a nit.
179de9c0bb: The sample is the evidence. The two groups have the same confidence, so any cutoff removes both. A and C bet on a number the model produces about itself. Calibration would need a validation set per category, which is more work than writing the category definition. D is the same idea with a different scale. B fixes the boundary where it’s defined, and measures it from outside the model.
f39f6041d2: “Truly critical” is just another adjective (A). B follows the guide (explicit severity criteria with code examples) and adds two structural controls. Severity belongs to the rule, so the model can’t inflate it. And style is removed from scope entirely. C makes the problem worse. D adds a second boundary with the same undefined definition.
e848597e04:
The guide’s condition is met: detailed instructions have already produced inconsistent results. Its prescription is two to four targeted examples for the ambiguous cases, showing acceptable versus genuine, with the reason.

A is too many, and mostly obvious. C reduces sampling variance but doesn’t move the boundary; a deterministic wrong decision is still wrong. D reduces variance by voting. It costs three calls, and the majority still gets the boundary wrong.
adc3b38c29:
The model invents because the schema requires a value, and no example shows that “none” is acceptable. B changes both.

A rewards fabrication. The information isn’t in the source, so retries (Chapter 12) can’t find it. C is unrelated. D catches malformed numbers, but not a well-formed identifier from the wrong field. It’s a good additional check, not the fix.
aaf8540174: This is one of the official sample answers. Sentiment correlates with escalation, but it isn’t the criterion. So A fails both the “upset but resolvable” case and the “calm but explicit request” case. Self-reported confidence is an unreliable trigger (C). A trained classifier (D) is heavy machinery for a problem that explicit criteria and examples solve, and it doesn’t make the criteria inspectable.
f6e3674c67:
The measured problem is one category, with enough comments (n = 120) to act on. B is the guide’s “temporarily disable high false-positive categories while improving prompts”, with the evidence and the exit path.

A throws away three good rules. C is the vague instruction again. D abandons a rule whose real defects the team wants; a swallowed exception does lose failure signals. The rule just needs better criteria. R4’s n of 23 is too small to act on either way, so it stays.
af83442265: Use the companion folder ccarf-companion/11-criteria-few-shot/. Everything runs offline. Add --live, with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set, to run the same prompts against the real model. Assertions then report differences instead of failing.
5354a73d74: In review_lib.py, add a fifth rule R5 with severity and text (for example, a Kafka listener that commits the offset before the database write). Add a labelled defect and a labelled near miss to review_data.py, and re-run example 01. Which prompt change did the near miss need?
d2cc293b33: Run 13_generalization_holdout.py. Add a held-out near miss of your own, for example a constant referenced through an interface. Also add a held-out defect that an over-broad constant exemption might hide (String.valueOf(request.getParameter("x"))). Does the simulation handle them? What does the answer tell you about testing real prompts?
833826bb43:
Done when you can:

  • write report-if rules, a skip list and severity anchors for a new reviewer from a blank page;
  • compute and explain per-rule precision with an interval, and decide from it whether to disable a category;
  • pick two to four examples from a failure log, justify each, and show a held-out test for generalisation;
  • explain, for each of the exam traps above, which sentence of the official task statement rules it out.
